claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
subclaims: What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?
Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations eliminated during a successful jailbreak attack?
Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations bypassed during a successful jailbreak attack?
Does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress a small subset of attention heads?
Is suppressing that subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?
Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?
Can the persistent internal representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?
Is additional training required to read out those representations as a harmful-input detector?
How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?

experiments: To address subclaim "What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?" and the paired subclaims "Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations eliminated during a successful jailbreak attack?" and "Are the model’s safety-relevant internal representations bypassed during a successful jailbreak attack?", run a representational comparison study on a publicly available safety-aligned model and jailbreak benchmark. Use a model such as Llama-2-7b-chat or Mistral-7B-Instruct, and prompts from HarmBench, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench (all public). Construct matched prompt sets: benign, plainly harmful, and harmful-with-jailbreak-suffix/prefix that empirically convert refusals into compliant answers. For each prompt, record hidden states and attention-head outputs across layers while generating the first refusal/compliance tokens. First identify candidate safety-relevant directions by contrasting activations for benign vs harmful non-jailbroken prompts that the model refuses; this can be done with simple unsupervised or linear-probe-free diagnostics such as mean-difference directions, CKA similarity to harmful/non-harmful centroids, or activation steering directions derived only from class means. Then test whether those directions disappear under successful jailbreaks or remain present. Also quantify whether the final behavior shifts despite persistence of those directions. A key control is to compare successful jailbreaks against unsuccessful jailbreak attempts and against direct harmful prompts answered with refusal. If the harmful-associated directions remain strong under successful jailbreaks, while output behavior changes from refusal to compliance, that supports the "bypass" view rather than elimination. If those directions collapse to benign-like values during successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination. Intermediate results, such as persistence in mid-layers but disappearance near the output, would suggest partial bypass localized late in computation rather than global preservation. This experiment is highest priority because it establishes whether there is anything persistent to read out or causally intervene on. It could be made partly unnecessary if strong prior evidence already included layerwise activation traces on matched harmful, jailbroken, and benign prompts showing persistence or disappearance of safety-relevant directions across the network.

To address subclaim "Does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress a small subset of attention heads?" and "Is suppressing that subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?", perform a causal head-ablation and rescue experiment. Using the same public model and jailbreak datasets, first identify attention heads whose outputs change most between harmful-refusal prompts and their successfully jailbroken counterparts; prioritize heads showing large, consistent reduction under jailbreak specifically on harmful inputs. Rank heads by effect size, then intervene at inference time: (1) suppress only the top-k candidate heads during normal harmful prompts that would otherwise be refused, by zeroing or mean-patching their output vectors; (2) restore those same heads during successful jailbreak prompts by activation patching from the matched non-jailbroken harmful-refusal run; and (3) include controls that suppress random head sets of the same size, suppress MLP channels instead, or suppress candidate heads on benign tasks to test specificity. Measure refusal/compliance rate, harmfulness score of completions using a public evaluator or rubric, and perplexity impact on benign tasks from a public corpus such as WikiText or AlpacaEval-style harmless prompts. If suppressing a very small head subset reliably flips refusal to compliance, while random subsets do not, that supports selective suppression being sufficient. If restoring those heads during jailbroken runs reinstates refusal, that strengthens a causal interpretation. If many heads must be suppressed, or random subsets work similarly, the "small selective subset" claim weakens. If suppressing candidate heads broadly degrades model quality, the effect may reflect generic damage rather than safety-specific gating. This experiment could be made less necessary if existing evidence already provided causal activation-patching or ablation results demonstrating both sufficiency and rescue for a compact head set across multiple jailbreak families.

To address subclaim "Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?", "Can the persistent internal representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?", "Is additional training required to read out those representations as a harmful-input detector?", and "How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?", build a zero-additional-training detection benchmark from internal activations. Use public harmfulness datasets such as HarmBench, BeaverTails, ToxicChat, and WildJailbreak/JailbreakBench to create a held-out mixture of benign prompts, harmful prompts, and successfully jailbroken harmful prompts. From the model under test, extract activations from non-suppressed heads and/or layers identified in Experiment 1 as still encoding harmfulness during jailbreak. Define a detector without fitting new parameters on labeled data: for example, score each input by cosine similarity to a harmful centroid computed from a small reference set, by projection onto a precomputed harmful-minus-benign mean direction from the model’s own refusal regime, or by aggregation of head-level harmfulness scores discovered in Experiment 1. Compare this zero-training detector against dedicated public safety classifiers such as Llama Guard, OpenAI moderation analogs where open equivalents exist, Detoxify, or other HuggingFace safety models, using AUROC, AUPRC, F1 at fixed false-positive rate, and robustness specifically on jailbroken prompts. Include a stricter no-training variant where the harmful direction is inferred only from paired harmful/benign prompt templates rather than any supervised fitting, plus a light-training baseline (e.g., logistic regression on frozen activations) to show the gap if any. If the zero-training internal detector performs competitively with dedicated safety models, especially on successfully jailbroken inputs, that supports the claim strongly. If it only works after fitting a classifier, the "no additional training" claim fails but persistence may still hold. If dedicated safety models far outperform it, the competitiveness claim weakens. This experiment becomes less necessary if prior evidence already reports strong held-out benchmarking of a training-free activation-based detector against public safety baselines on standard jailbreak and harmfulness datasets.

To address subclaim 1/2/3/6 — whether safety-relevant internal representations persist during a successful jailbreak, are bypassed rather than eliminated, and remain present in heads outside the putatively suppressed subset — run a comparative activation-analysis study on a public safety-aligned open-weight model such as Llama-2-Chat or Llama-3-Instruct. Use a public harmfulness/jailbreak corpus combining AdvBench, HarmBench, and a public jailbreak-prompt set such as JailbreakHub-style prompts from HuggingFace/Kaggle. Construct matched triplets: (a) harmful request that elicits refusal, (b) the same harmful request embedded in a successful jailbreak that elicits compliance, and (c) benign controls. First identify candidate safety-relevant directions/features from the refusal condition using unsupervised or minimally supervised methods already available for the model family: e.g., layerwise linear probes trained only on the refusal-vs-benign contrast, sparse autoencoder features if public SAEs exist, or direct mean-difference directions between harmful and benign prompts. Then test whether those same directions/features remain decodable in the successful-jailbreak condition by measuring separability of harmful vs benign inputs from hidden states and attention-head outputs at each layer, including after conditioning on output behavior. Critically, compare two hypotheses: elimination predicts the harmfulness signal collapses toward benign under jailbreak; bypass predicts strong harmfulness signal remains in many internal locations despite compliant output. A stronger causal version is to activation-patch hidden states from refusal runs into corresponding positions in jailbreak runs and see whether harmfulness features restore refusal only when patched into late decision-relevant sites, not when patched into already signal-rich representational sites. If harmfulness signals remain linearly readable across many layers and heads during successful jailbreaks, that supports bypass over elimination; if signals vanish broadly, that supports elimination. If only a narrow late-stage bottleneck changes while earlier harmfulness encoding persists, that would be especially strong evidence for bypass. This experiment could become partly unnecessary if a paper already released layerwise activation comparisons on matched refusal/jailbreak pairs together with open activations and causal interventions showing signal persistence.

To address subclaim 4/5 — whether a jailbreak selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and whether suppressing that subset alone is sufficient to flip refusal to compliance — perform a causal head-localization and intervention experiment. On the same public aligned model and matched refusal/jailbreak dataset, use attribution patching, direct activation patching, and head ablation to rank attention heads by how much their output changes the refusal/compliance logit gap between the refusal and jailbreak conditions. Define the candidate suppressed subset as the minimal set of heads whose outputs are consistently reduced or redirected in successful jailbreaks and whose patching from refusal into jailbreak restores refusal-related logits. Then intervene in both directions: (1) suppress only this subset in otherwise non-jailbroken harmful prompts, via zeroing head outputs, mean-ablation, or rescaling their value vectors, and test whether refusals become compliant; (2) restore only this subset in jailbreak runs and test whether compliance reverts to refusal. Evaluate subset size, robustness across prompt families, and transfer across multiple jailbreak styles, including suffix, roleplay, and multi-turn attacks. The key criterion is minimal sufficiency: can a small head set, much smaller than all attention heads, account for most of the behavior change? If suppressing a compact subset reliably turns refusals into compliance, and restoring that subset undoes successful jailbreaks, the claim’s selective-suppression mechanism gains strong causal support. If many heads across many layers must be perturbed, or no compact subset is sufficient, the claim is weakened. If suppression correlates with behavior but intervention is not sufficient, the heads may be markers rather than causes. This experiment could be made less necessary if there were already public causal-ablation results across several jailbreak families demonstrating a consistent minimal head set with bidirectional control over refusal/compliance.

To address subclaim 7/8/9 — whether the persistent internal representations can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, without additional training, and at quality competitive with dedicated safety models — build a zero- or near-zero-training detector from the representations found in Experiment 1 and benchmark it against public safety baselines. Use public datasets with harmful/benign labels, such as HarmBench, AdvBench, ToxicChat, BeaverTails, and jailbreak corpora containing both successful and unsuccessful attacks. For the no-additional-training version, derive a detector score directly from fixed internal directions/features: for example, cosine similarity to a harmfulness direction estimated once from a small public calibration split or even from hand-specified harmful categories; aggregate scores across the persistent heads/layers identified earlier. Then compare against stronger but still lightweight baselines, such as frozen linear probes trained on small labeled sets, and dedicated safety models/classifiers available publicly on HuggingFace (for example toxicity or harmfulness classifiers, Llama Guard–style open models if available, or DeBERTa/RoBERTa safety classifiers). Evaluate AUROC, AUPRC, calibration, false-positive rate on benign but sensitive prompts, and robustness specifically on successful jailbreak inputs where output-based moderation often fails. If a direct readout with no extra training matches or approaches dedicated safety models, especially on successful-jailbreak detection, that strongly supports the claim. If it requires substantial supervised fitting, then the “no additional training” part is false even if the representations are useful. If it performs much worse than dedicated safety models, the competitiveness claim is weakened. This experiment could be partly unnecessary if an existing paper already published reproducible benchmarks showing zero-training internal-state detectors on public models and datasets outperforming or matching standard safety classifiers.

To address subclaim 1/2/3/4/6 — that successful jailbreaks bypass rather than eliminate safety-relevant internal representations, and do so by selectively suppressing a small subset of attention heads while other heads continue to represent harmful content — run a multi-model mechanistic intervention study on a public harmful-instruction benchmark. Use at least one open safety-aligned model with accessible internals (e.g., a Llama-2-Chat or similar HuggingFace chat model) and evaluate paired prompts from AdvBench and JailbreakBench: each harmful instruction in a non-adversarial baseline form and in a successful jailbreak form produced by a standardized attack such as GCG. Use deterministic decoding and a calibrated judge validated on a human-labeled subset to identify clean refusals versus jailbreak-induced compliances. First, localize candidate attention heads by contrasting activations between baseline harmful prompts that elicit refusal and jailbreaked versions that elicit compliance, focusing on heads whose outputs are consistently reduced under jailbreak while the semantic harmfulness of the user request is unchanged. Then test causality with path patching, zero-ablation, and activation scaling: (i) zero or downscale only the candidate heads during the non-jailbroken harmful prompt and measure whether refusal flips to compliance; (ii) restore or upscale those same heads during the jailbreak prompt and test whether compliance flips back to refusal; (iii) compare against size-matched random-head ablations and layer-matched controls. In parallel, test whether other heads still encode harmfulness during successful jailbreaks by attempting a no-training linear readout directly from existing head activations or attention outputs: compute class separation/AUROC for harmful versus benign inputs using raw projection directions or simple frozen probes derived only from prompt-pair differences, without optimizing model parameters, and compare representations under successful jailbreak versus ordinary refusal. Include benign controls from Alpaca to quantify collateral capability degradation and false positives. If targeted suppression is sufficient to flip refusal to compliance, restoration reverses jailbreaks, random ablations do not, and harmfulness remains linearly separable in other heads during successful jailbreaks, that supports the bypass claim over the elimination claim. If instead harmfulness separability broadly collapses under jailbreak, or many random ablations produce the same effect, that would favor elimination or nonspecific damage. Stronger pre-existing evidence could make parts of this experiment unnecessary if there were already published, reproducible head-level causal maps and cross-validated demonstrations that harmfulness readouts remain stable under jailbreaked prompts.

To address subclaim 5 — that suppressing the identified subset of attention heads is by itself enough to turn a refusal into compliance — perform a sufficiency-and-specificity dose–response experiment using only standard harmful prompts, without any adversarial jailbreak string. On a chosen open model, begin with harmful requests from AdvBench that reliably produce refusals under deterministic decoding. Using the candidate head subset from Experiment 1, intervene at inference time by scaling those heads’ outputs with w in {1, 0.5, 0, -0.5 if numerically stable} while leaving all other components untouched. Measure ASR, refusal rate, KL shift in output distribution, and performance on matched harmless prompts from Alpaca. Compare with three controls expected in the subfield: baseline unmodified inference, size-matched random-head suppression, and suppression of equally salient but non-safety-related heads chosen from benign-prompt contrasts. Optionally test whether combining partial suppression of several heads is necessary, or whether a very small subset (e.g., top-k heads) alone produces the effect, by sweeping k. The key question is whether selective suppression alone, in the absence of any jailbreak prompt text, reliably induces compliance on harmful instructions while preserving relatively normal behavior on harmless tasks. If yes, that is strong evidence of sufficiency and specificity: the jailbreak likely works by functionally suppressing a refusal circuit rather than changing the task semantics. If compliance appears only when many heads are damaged or when harmless-task performance collapses, then the effect may reflect general capability degradation rather than a targeted refusal mechanism. If no suppression setting flips refusals to compliance, the original claim of sufficiency is weakened, even if those heads correlate with jailbreak success. This experiment could become less necessary if independent work had already shown robust causal dose–response curves and replication across labs that a tiny identified head set is sufficient to induce compliance without prompt-based jailbreaks.

To address subclaim 7/8/9 — that the persistent internal representations can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at quality competitive with dedicated safety models — run a frozen-feature harmful-input detection benchmark across public harmful and benign datasets. Use harmful inputs from AdvBench and JailbreakBench, benign instructions from Alpaca, and where possible include both plain harmful prompts and their jailbreaked variants that succeed behaviorally. From the open model studied above, extract the persistent representation identified as surviving successful jailbreaks (for example, activations of non-suppressed heads or layerwise residual directions shown to track harmfulness). Construct a training-free detector: examples include cosine similarity to a fixed harmfulness direction estimated from a small prompt-pair difference set, nearest-centroid scoring using centroids computed without optimization, or direct use of a single mechanistically identified scalar feature. Explicitly avoid gradient-based fitting or additional model training; if any calibration threshold is needed, choose it on a tiny public validation split and report sensitivity to threshold choice. Evaluate AUROC, FPR at fixed TPR, and calibration-like operating characteristics for distinguishing harmful from benign prompts, including the subset of harmful prompts that successfully jailbreak the model. Compare these scores against dedicated safety baselines available via APIs or public models, such as OpenAI Moderation and LlamaGuard-like open alternatives where feasible, using identical prompt sets. Also compare to a trivial lexical baseline to show the detector is not merely keyword spotting. If the frozen internal readout performs well on both ordinary and jailbreaked harmful prompts and is competitive with dedicated safety models, that supports the claim that safety-relevant representations persist and are directly usable without additional training. If performance drops sharply on successful jailbreaks, that would suggest the representations are not robustly persistent. If strong performance requires fitting a probe or substantial threshold tuning, the no-additional-training claim is weakened. This experiment could be partly unnecessary if there were already externally replicated benchmark results showing a clearly specified zero-training internal detector matching or exceeding standard safety models on the same public datasets.

To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, and 9, run a representation-persistence and zero-shot detector study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, or Mistral-7B-Instruct. Use publicly available harmful/benign prompt datasets such as AdvBench, HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and Anthropic HH-RLHF harmless/helpful splits. For each harmful prompt, evaluate both the plain harmful prompt and one or more successful jailbreak wrappers, retaining only cases where the model refuses the plain prompt but complies under the jailbreak. Record hidden states, attention-head outputs, and attention patterns at each layer/head. Test whether harmful-content representations persist by using no-training or near-zero-training readouts: for example, compute activation-direction prototypes from benign versus harmful plain prompts, or use cosine similarity to harmful-prompt centroids, then evaluate whether these same directions still classify jailbreak-wrapped harmful prompts as harmful. Compare AUROC/AUPRC/F1 against public dedicated safety classifiers such as Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, or Detoxify on the same held-out prompts. If harmful-vs-benign separability remains high in internal activations during successful jailbreaks, and a frozen/prototype readout is competitive with dedicated safety models, that supports persistence and direct readability; if separability collapses specifically on successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination rather than bypass. If the readout requires supervised fitting on many jailbreak examples to work, that weakens the no-additional-training subclaim. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by stronger existing evidence consisting of released activation datasets from successful jailbreaks plus benchmarked zero-shot readout scores against safety classifiers.

To address subclaims 3, 4, 5, and 6, perform causal head-identification and intervention experiments on successful jailbreak cases. Using the same public datasets and models, first identify attention heads whose outputs or attention patterns differ most between refusal cases and successful jailbreak-compliance cases, controlling for prompt length and wrapper tokens. Rank heads by causal importance using activation patching or path patching: patch each head from the plain-refusal run into the jailbreak run, and separately patch from the jailbreak run into the plain run, measuring refusal/compliance probability, harmful-answer likelihood, and generated output judged by HarmBench or Llama Guard. Then test whether the claimed small subset is sufficient by directly suppressing, ablating, or scaling down that subset during ordinary harmful prompts that would otherwise be refused, and observing whether refusal turns into compliance. Also test whether non-suppressed heads still encode harmful content by applying the detector/readout from experiment 1 to activations with the candidate heads ablated. If only a small ranked subset causally flips refusal to compliance and other heads retain harmful-content separability, that supports selective bypass; if many heads are required, the effect is diffuse, or suppressing the subset does not induce compliance, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by existing causal-intervention evidence that reports exact head indices, ablation strengths, and refusal-to-compliance flip rates across multiple models and jailbreak types.

To address subclaims 4, 5, 7, 8, and 9 across robustness and generality, replicate the strongest findings from experiments 1 and 2 across different jailbreak families, model families, and held-out datasets. Use public jailbreak templates from JailbreakBench, HarmBench, and repositories of DAN/roleplay/encoding jailbreaks, and test at least two safety-aligned open models. Split attacks into seen and unseen families; identify the suppressible head subset on one attack family and dataset, then evaluate whether the same subset and zero-shot harmful detector transfer to unseen attacks, unseen harmful categories, and another model of similar architecture where possible. Compare detector quality to dedicated safety models under distribution shift, including benign adversarial prompts that mention harmful topics in safe contexts. If the same small-head bypass mechanism and persistent readout generalize, the full claim becomes much more feasible; if head subsets are attack-specific, model-specific, or fail on benign hard negatives, the claim may hold only narrowly. This experiment could be reduced or skipped if experiments 1 and 2 already show broad multi-model, multi-attack generalization with public code, prompts, and activation logs.

To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 6, 7, 8, and 9, run a paired activation/readout study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, or Mistral-Instruct. Use public harmful-intent datasets such as HarmBench or AdvBench, benign controls from Alpaca/ShareGPT, and public jailbreak templates or labeled attacks from JailbreakBench/JailbreakHub. For each harmful request, create paired inputs: the plain harmful request, a jailbreak-wrapped version that actually elicits non-refusal, and benign controls with similar surface form. Record residual-stream states and per-head outputs at each layer during the prompt and early generation. Then test whether harmfulness remains linearly or directly readable in successful jailbreak cases using only pre-specified, non-trained readouts: e.g., logit-lens scores for fixed unsafe-category label tokens, cosine similarity to unembedding-derived harmfulness/refusal directions, or nearest-neighbor retrieval against frozen model activations without fitting parameters. Evaluate whether these readouts distinguish successful jailbroken harmful inputs from benign inputs, and compare AUROC/F1 to public dedicated safety classifiers such as Llama Guard, ShieldGemma, or HarmBench classifiers. If harmfulness is still detectable in successful jailbreak activations at competitive quality, this supports persistence and direct readout; if detection collapses to benign levels, this supports elimination or strong obfuscation; if only trained probes work, it weakens the no additional training subclaim. This experiment could be made unnecessary by publicly released activation traces and train-free detector benchmarks showing the same comparison on matched successful jailbreaks and benign controls.

To address subclaims 4 and 5, perform causal head-localization and intervention experiments on the same successful jailbreak/plain-refusal prompt pairs. First identify candidate attention heads whose outputs, attention patterns, or activation norms are selectively reduced during successful jailbreak prompts relative to plain harmful prompts that refuse, while controlling for prompt length and position. Rank heads using activation patching, attribution patching, or path patching with refusal/compliance logit-difference as the metric. Then test causality: suppress only the top-k candidate heads on plain harmful prompts by zero-ablation or mean-ablation and measure whether the model changes from refusal toward compliance; conversely, restore or patch those heads from the plain-refusal run into the jailbroken run and measure whether refusal returns. Vary k to test the small subset claim. If a small, stable set of heads is both selectively suppressed by jailbreaks and causally sufficient to flip refusal/compliance, the subclaims are supported; if many heads are required, the effect is diffuse; if suppression is correlational and patching does not change behavior, the claim is weakened. This experiment could be made unnecessary by a reproducible circuit-discovery artifact giving head indices, patching code, and intervention effect sizes across public models and datasets.

With respect to evidence pieces 8 and 9, test whether the proposed bypass mechanism generalizes beyond one attack family by repeating the activation and head-intervention analyses across different jailbreak types, including multi-turn attention-shifting attacks and continuation-triggered jailbreaks, using public datasets or prompts from JailbreakBench, HarmBench, and the papers' released artifacts if available. For each attack class, measure three quantities on matched successful and failed attacks: persistence of harmful-content readouts in non-suppressed heads, suppression magnitude of the candidate refusal-mediating heads, and causal flip rates under head ablation/restoration. Also test cross-attack transfer: heads discovered on one jailbreak type should predict or causally affect behavior on another if the claim describes a general mechanism. If the same small head subset and persistent harmful representations appear across attack families and models, the broad bypass account is strengthened; if each attack uses different components, the claim may hold only locally; if continuation or multi-turn attacks show representation loss rather than bypass, the general claim fails. This experiment could be made unnecessary by stronger existing evidence from papers 8 and 9 reporting cross-attack, cross-model causal interventions rather than only behavioral jailbreak success rates.

To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, and 6, run a representation-persistence study on open safety-aligned models with accessible activations, such as Llama-2-7B-Chat, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, and Vicuna. Use paired harmful instructions from AdvBench and JailbreakBench in three forms: plain harmful prompt expected to be refused, the same harmful prompt wrapped in successful jailbreak templates or public GCG-style adversarial prompts, and matched benign prompts from Alpaca/XSTest. Decode deterministically and label refusal/compliance with a human-calibrated judge. For each attention head, compare activations and attention outputs across plain-harmful-refused, jailbroken-harmful-complied, and benign conditions; use activation patching/path patching to test whether heads that encode harmfulness in the refused condition still carry similar information in the successful jailbreak condition. Results supporting bypass rather than elimination would show that many harmfulness-sensitive heads remain closer to the plain harmful condition than to benign prompts even when ASR is high, while the downstream refusal behavior changes. Results supporting elimination would show harmfulness-sensitive representations collapsing to benign-like states during successful jailbreaks. If a released activation dataset already demonstrated this persistence across models, attacks, and human-validated success labels, this experiment could be reduced to replication on additional model families.

To address subclaims 4 and 5, identify whether a small subset of attention heads is selectively suppressed by successful jailbreaks and whether suppressing that subset is sufficient to convert refusal into compliance. Starting from the paired runs in Experiment 1, rank heads by jailbreak-induced reduction in output norm, attention contribution, or causal effect on refusal logits using activation patching/ACDC threshold sweeps. Select the smallest high-effect subset and intervene at inference on plain harmful prompts by zeroing or scaling those heads down to their jailbroken activation levels; also perform the inverse intervention by restoring or scaling up those heads during jailbroken prompts. Compare ASR, refusal rate, KL divergence, and harmless-prompt performance against unmodified inference, size-matched random head ablations, and ablations of heads with similar magnitude but low causal score. The claim is supported if targeted suppression alone produces a large refusal-to-compliance shift, random matched ablations do not, restoring the heads reduces jailbreak ASR, and Alpaca/benign performance is not broadly degraded. The claim is weakened if many heads are required, effects match random ablation, or the intervention mainly causes general incoherence. This experiment could be made partly unnecessary by stronger prior evidence releasing the exact head set plus dose-response and random-ablation controls across several public benchmarks.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, evaluate whether the persistent internal representations can serve as a no-additional-training harmful-input detector competitive with dedicated safety models. Using only the heads/features identified in Experiments 1 and 2, predefine a direct readout score such as the aggregate activation magnitude or cosine similarity of the persistent harmfulness-representing heads, without fitting a classifier; if a binary threshold is needed, report both threshold-free AUROC/AUPRC and a calibration-only threshold chosen before the held-out test. Evaluate on held-out harmful prompts from AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and HarmBench, plus benign/ambiguous prompts from Alpaca and XSTest, including both plain and jailbroken variants. Compare against dedicated or commonly used safety systems such as LlamaGuard, WildGuard, OpenAI Moderation where available, and a calibrated GPT-4-class judge, using AUROC, FPR at fixed TPR, precision/recall, and robustness to jailbreak wrappers. The claim is supported if the direct internal readout detects harmful intent in successful jailbreaks with performance close to these safety models and without supervised probe training; it is weakened if performance requires a trained classifier, fails on held-out attacks, or has high benign false positives. This experiment could be made unnecessary if a public benchmark already released the frozen readout rule, held-out prompts, labels, and head activations showing competitive zero-shot detection across models.

To address subclaims 1, 2, 3, 4, and 6, map safety representations before and during successful jailbreaks in two open-weight aligned models, such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Construct matched triplets consisting of a plainly stated harmful request, a successful jailbreak preserving the same request, and a benign length/topic-matched prompt, using public HarmBench and JailbreakBench behaviors and attacks; verify success with the public HarmBench classifier plus blinded human review of a sample. Cache every attention-head output and residual-stream state. On a discovery split, define each head's safety direction from refused harmful prompts versus benign prompts, then test on held-out behaviors whether jailbreaks selectively reduce projection onto that direction. Separately measure harmful-content decodability from every head and layer using cross-validated linear probes, with attack families held out to prevent wrapper memorization. Predefine 'small subset' as no more than 5% of heads and 'selective suppression' as that subset explaining most of the jailbreak-associated loss of refusal-direction signal after false-discovery correction. Persistence would be supported if successful jailbreaks reduce safety-routing signals in a small subset while harmfulness remains decodable from many other heads at approximately the level seen for unjailbroken harmful prompts; loss of decodability across the network would instead support elimination, while diffuse changes would refute selective suppression. Publicly released, prompt-level activation traces covering the same models and matched conditions could make new inference runs unnecessary, although the analyses would still need to be reproduced.

To address subclaim 5 and strengthen subclaims 3 and 4 causally, intervene on the head subset identified in Experiment 1 using a completely held-out portion of HarmBench and JailbreakBench. For plain harmful prompts that normally elicit refusal, zero, mean-ablate, or remove only the refusal-direction component of those heads during generation, and measure whether outputs change to substantive harmful compliance. For successful jailbreaks, perform the reverse intervention by activation-patching the corresponding head components from the matched refused prompt and test whether refusal is restored. Include equal-sized random-head subsets, activation-norm-matched subsets, heads selected for general language modeling importance, sham hooks, benign prompts, and subset-size dose-response curves. Score refusal, compliance, and harmfulness with the HarmBench classifier, blinded human ratings, and benign utility/perplexity controls; preregister a large causal criterion, such as the selected subset producing a substantially greater compliance change than 95% of matched random subsets without broad degradation. If suppressing the small subset reliably converts refusals to harmful compliance and restoring it reverses jailbreaks, the bypass mechanism and sufficiency claim gain strong support. If only broad ablation works, if random heads work equally well, or if outputs merely become incoherent, the claim is not supported. Public intervention logs containing per-prompt outputs for selected and matched-control heads could substitute for rerunning generation if they include all stated controls.

To address subclaims 7, 8, and 9, freeze the persistent heads and representation locations found in Experiment 1, then evaluate a genuinely label-free direct readout on previously unseen attack families and datasets. Use a preregistered logit-lens score: apply the model's existing layer normalization and unembedding to each selected internal state, compute fixed log-odds for model-tokenized harmful/unsafe versus harmless/safe verbalizers, aggregate across heads with a fixed median or maximum, and use a zero threshold without fitting weights or thresholds. Test on public WildGuardMix, XSTest, HarmBench, and JailbreakBench splits with behavior and attack-family separation. Compare this no-training detector against a supervised linear probe on the same activations, simple output/refusal heuristics, and publicly available dedicated safety models such as Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, and WildGuard. Report AUROC, AUPRC, balanced accuracy, calibration, and true-positive rate at fixed 1% and 5% false-positive rates, including benign hard negatives and successful jailbreaks; define competitiveness in advance with a noninferiority margin, for example no more than three percentage points below the best dedicated model on macro-averaged AUROC and fixed-FPR recall. Competitive performance from the frozen zero-training score would support direct readout without additional training; success only after fitting a probe would show that representations persist but refute the no-additional-training claim; poor performance from both would undermine detector feasibility. A public benchmark submission containing frozen readout code, untouched test predictions, and scores against the same baselines could remove the need to repeat this evaluation.

To address subclaims 1–4 and 6, run a paired activation study on open-weight safety-aligned models such as Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Use harmful intents from the publicly available HarmBench or AdvBench datasets, matched benign prompts from XSTest, and jailbreak transformations from JailbreakBench/JailbreakHub. Retain only triples consisting of a harmful request that is refused, a jailbreak version of the same request that succeeds according to both HarmBench’s classifier and blinded human review, and a benign control. Record every attention head’s output and the residual stream at each generated token. Define safety-relevant directions using only a separate set of clean harmful-versus-benign prompts, then test whether those directions still decode harmfulness during successful jailbreaks; quantify per-head changes relative to the paired refused prompt and test whether suppression is concentrated in a small subset rather than distributed across the network. Include lexical-template-held-out, attack-family-held-out, and model-held-out analyses to prevent jailbreak wording from masquerading as harmfulness. Persistent decodability in residual streams and many unaffected heads, alongside concentrated suppression in a few heads, would support bypass rather than elimination; loss of decodability across components would support elimination, while diffuse changes would reject the small-subset claim. Public release of paired successful-jailbreak activations and equivalent layer/head-level analyses across several models could make this experiment largely unnecessary.

To address subclaims 3–5, perform preregistered causal interventions using the candidate heads localized in Experiment 1. On clean harmful prompts that normally elicit refusal, suppress each candidate head and combinations of candidates by zero ablation, mean ablation, or removal of only its projection onto the independently identified safety direction; measure changes in refusal rate, harmful-compliance rate, and next-token refusal logits. Conversely, during successful jailbreaks, activation-patch those heads from the matched refused execution or restore their safety-direction component and test whether refusal returns. Compare against equal-sized random-head sets, heads matched for activation magnitude and layer, benign prompts, and sham patches; search for the minimum sufficient subset on one partition of HarmBench and confirm it unchanged on held-out HarmBench categories, AdvBench, and JailbreakBench attack families. A small subset whose suppression reliably converts refusal to harmful compliance, and whose restoration reverses successful jailbreaks without broadly damaging benign capability, would provide strong causal evidence for selective bypass. Failure of targeted interventions, equivalence to random ablations, or a need to suppress many heads would refute or substantially narrow the claim. This experiment could be replaced by publicly available, reproducible intervention traces demonstrating both necessity and sufficiency with matched random controls.

To address subclaims 6–9, evaluate a genuinely training-free internal harmful-input detector. Precommit to a direct logit-lens score: at a fixed token position, project each residual stream or individual head output through the model’s existing normalization and unembedding matrix, and score the logit difference between a fixed, model-independent set of unsafe tokens (for example, “harmful” and “unsafe”) and safe tokens (for example, “harmless” and “safe”); choose the layer by a non-label-based rule such as the final pre-generation layer, and use a zero threshold so that no probe fitting, threshold calibration, or labeled training occurs. Evaluate this score on clean and successfully jailbroken harmful prompts from held-out HarmBench, JailbreakBench, and AdvBench, with benign and over-refusal controls from XSTest and WildGuardMix, reporting AUROC, AUPRC, false-positive rate at fixed recall, attack-family generalization, bootstrap confidence intervals, and per-model results. Compare on exactly the same examples with publicly available dedicated safety models such as Llama-Guard-3, ShieldGemma, and WildGuard, while separately reporting their parameter and training advantages. Strong detection of successful jailbreak inputs and statistically comparable performance to these guards would support persistence, direct readout, and competitive quality without additional training; good linear-probe performance but weak fixed-logit-lens performance would show that representations persist but require training, and poor performance from both would undermine direct detectability. A published benchmark already reporting training-free internal readouts and matched dedicated-guard results on unseen attacks could obviate this experiment.

To address subclaim “safety-relevant representations are not eliminated but bypassed, with only a small subset of attention heads suppressed,” run paired representational and circuit-discovery analyses on at least two open safety-aligned checkpoints, such as Llama-2-7B-Chat and Llama-2-13B-Chat. Use harmful instructions from the public AdvBench and JailbreakBench datasets, generate GCG and standard template jailbreaks, and retain same-instruction pairs in which the ordinary prompt is refused but the jailbreak succeeds under deterministic decoding. Calibrate the success judge against human labels before analysis. Record every head’s output, norm, and projection onto harmfulness and refusal directions for ordinary harmful prompts, successful jailbreaks, failed jailbreaks, and benign Alpaca controls. Train diagnostic probes only on ordinary harmful-versus-benign examples and test them, without refitting, on successful jailbreak activations; this tests whether harmful-content information persists out of distribution. In parallel, use ACDC, attribution patching, and HISP with sparsity sweeps to identify heads whose safety-related output is consistently reduced specifically during successful attacks. Require a quantitatively small set, stability across attacks and data splits, and stronger suppression than size-matched random or activation-magnitude-matched heads. Persistence of cross-condition probe accuracy in most heads, alongside concentrated suppression of a small refusal-associated subset, would support bypass rather than representational erasure; broad loss of decodability would support elimination, while diffuse changes would reject the selective-suppression claim. Replication across checkpoints would strengthen generality, whereas inconsistent head identities but consistent functional roles would support only a functional, not anatomical, version of the claim. This experiment could be reduced or skipped if public paired clean/jailbroken activation traces with independently validated success labels and full per-head measurements already existed for the same checkpoints and benchmarks.

To address subclaim “suppressing the identified subset of attention heads is sufficient to turn refusal into compliance,” intervene on the heads selected using only the discovery split from the first experiment. On held-out AdvBench and JailbreakBench instructions that the unmodified model refuses, scale those head outputs through w ∈ {0, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2} at every relevant prompt and generation position, and separately patch in the head values observed during the matched successful jailbreak. Measure refusal rate, policy-relevant compliance, response relevance, and output KL under deterministic decoding, using a human-calibrated judge. Test the reverse intervention as well: during an actual jailbreak, patch the selected heads from the matched ordinary refused run or amplify them, asking whether refusal is restored. Include unmodified inference, size- and layer-matched random heads, globally high-magnitude heads, failed-jailbreak pairs, and benign Alpaca prompts; measure benign instruction-following and general output degradation so that indiscriminate model damage cannot masquerade as a safety effect. A large, dose-dependent rise in relevant harmful compliance from suppressing only the selected heads, together with restoration of refusal when their clean activations are patched back, would provide evidence for causal sufficiency and a bypass mechanism. An effect no larger than random ablation, an effect requiring many heads, or broad degradation on benign prompts would refute or substantially narrow the claim. Existing public intervention results would make this unnecessary only if they include held-out causal ablations, reverse patching, random-head controls, benign-task controls, and human-validated compliance labels rather than correlational activation measurements alone.

To address subclaim “the persistent representations can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, without additional training, at quality competitive with dedicated safety models,” freeze the checkpoints, layers, and persistent-head set before detector evaluation and construct a strictly parameter-free score from prompt-time activations only—for example, the mean normalized projection of the persistent heads onto a harmful-versus-harmless direction exposed through the model’s native unembedding, with no learned probe, tuned lens, gradient updates, or response tokens. Evaluate clean and jailbroken harmful inputs from held-out AdvBench and JailbreakBench against benign Alpaca inputs, with deduplication from circuit discovery and separate reporting for ordinary and successfully jailbroken prompts. Report AUROC and AUPRC, plus F1, false-positive rate, and false-negative rate at a preregistered zero threshold; if a threshold is calibrated, report it separately so it is not presented as a wholly training-free result. Compare under the same input-only protocol with publicly available dedicated models such as Llama Guard 3, ShieldGemma, and a public HarmBench classifier, using bootstrap confidence intervals and a preregistered non-inferiority margin such as three AUROC points. Also fit a conventional linear probe as an explicitly trained ceiling: if the parameter-free readout is weak but the probe is strong, the representations persist but additional training is required. Performance within the non-inferiority margin, including on successful jailbreaks and with acceptable benign false positives, would support the full detector claim; strong separability only after probe fitting would reject the no-additional-training subclaim, and poor performance for both readouts would undermine persistence or practical accessibility. This experiment could be replaced by a public, leakage-controlled benchmark containing frozen activation scores and predictions from the same dedicated safety baselines, provided the purported direct readout was fixed before its test set and truly used no fitted parameters.
